chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who is struck in the eye, so part of his vision is lost. What is given to him? He (peace be upon him) said: 'One of them (the eyes) is tied/covered, then an egg is placed for him, then it is said to him, "Look!" As long as he claims that he sees its place, (it is moved away) until it reaches a place where, if he passes it, he says, "I do not see it." It is brought nearer until he sees it, then that place is marked. Then it is measured with that measurement from behind him, and from his right, and from his left. So if it comes out equal, or else it is said to him, "You are lying," until he speaks the truth.' I said, 'Is he not trusted?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No, and there is no honor (guaranteed), and the same is done with the other eye. Then that is measured against the wergild (blood money) of the eye.'

key_terms.بَيْضَة: Egg (used as a visual reference object)
key_terms.كَلَامَة: Honor / Dignity (in the context of trusting the claimant)

ai.seo_question: How is partial blindness tested to determine compensation in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the precise forensic methodology employed by Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to assess partial visual impairment for 'diyah' (blood money) calculations, emphasizing empirical verification over mere claim. The procedure involves a controlled test using an egg to map the field of vision, ensuring the claimant's honesty through a 'lie detector' mechanism before measuring the defect against the other eye. This reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of integrating practical medical observation with legal jurisprudence to ensure equitable compensation.
